story.headline: Gold fell below $3,800, its lowest since September 2025, as the dollar firmed before the Fed's meeting minutes at 1:00 PM CT. UK inflation rose to 3.6%, as forecast, and the pound barely moved.

reads.policy: A December Fed rate hike is still seen as all but certain, and New York Fed President John Williams said one more is probably needed, but nothing dramatic. Europe, Britain and Japan are also expected to hike, while Canada and New Zealand look more likely to wait. US rates still look set to rise fastest, which keeps favouring the dollar.
reads.growth: Japan's exports hit a record in October on chip demand, a sign its economy is picking up after a small summer dip. In the US, shoppers keep spending while housing struggles. The US still looks firmer than most, which supports the dollar.
reads.inflation: UK inflation rose to 3.6% as expected, pushed up by fuel, while core prices stayed steady, so the pound got no new lift. Australian pay rose a bit faster than forecast, keeping alive the case for another rate hike there. Inflation is still well above target almost everywhere, which keeps most central banks leaning toward hikes.
reads.risk: Markets stayed nervous, with US stocks down for a second day and Iran attacking Bahrain again. Gold fell instead of rising, as some investors sold it to raise cash. The dollar gained from the unease, while the Aussie and kiwi, which track market mood, slipped.
reads.tot: Oil fell as US crude stocks rose, which takes a little away from the Canadian dollar. Gold's slide below $3,800 weighs on the Aussie, since Australia is a big gold producer. Cheaper oil helps importers such as the euro area and Japan.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds leaning toward the dollar and the pound and against the euro, the kiwi and the Canadian dollar, with bets against the kiwi growing fastest. Big long-term investors take the other side on the euro, pound and Aussie. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs above 5%, which weighs a little on trust in the dollar. France's debt troubles keep weighing on the euro.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. Hot inflation and firm consumer spending have made a December hike all but certain and kept the dollar near its highest since April 2025.
fed.priced: December: hike all but certain, with a half-point move only a small chance. More hikes expected next year.
fed.why: US inflation is running at about twice the Fed's 2% goal. New York Fed President John Williams says one more hike is probably needed, but nothing dramatic.
fed.watch: Minutes of the October meeting Wednesday, November 18 at 1:00 PM CT and weekly jobless claims Thursday, November 19 at 7:30 AM CT. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and said more may be needed. October inflation held at 3.1% with core prices near 2%, so a December hike now looks less likely than not.
boc.priced: December: hold more likely, with a hike a bit under even odds.
boc.why: Energy is lifting headline inflation, but core prices are calm and the economy is shedding jobs, so the bank can afford to wait.
boc.watch: Canada's November jobs figures on December 4 and the path of oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, and the kiwi has fallen to its lowest since 2020.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Businesses' inflation expectations barely moved and dairy prices were flat at the latest auction.
rbnz.watch: Governor Anna Breman speaks Wednesday, November 18 at 12:00 PM CT. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Economists see it as the last for now, which leaves the euro trailing as US rates keep rising, and it is hovering around $1.10.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, but factories are barely growing and France's debt worries linger, so the bank has little room to keep hiking.
ecb.watch: Final euro-area inflation for October Wednesday, November 18 at 4:00 AM CT and President Christine Lagarde at 8:25 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Record exports in October make a hike easier to justify after the economy shrank slightly in the summer.
boj.why: The weak yen is pushing import costs and prices up, and strong chip exports show the economy can take higher rates. The small summer contraction is the main reason to wait.
boj.watch: Whether Japan buys yen if the dollar tops 160 again, and Governor Kazuo Ueda's speech on November 30. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks, in a six-to-three vote. Big Australian banks think that is the peak, though pay rose a bit faster than forecast in the third quarter.
rba.priced: December: a hold expected, with rates seen at their peak.
rba.why: Most board members worry inflation is too high, and faster pay growth backs them. Three feared a sharper slowdown, and unemployment is at a five-year high.
rba.watch: October jobs figures Wednesday, November 18 at 6:30 PM CT. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5 and said more may follow. UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October, as forecast, so a second hike in December is still more likely than not.
boe.priced: December: a second hike more likely than not.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal. Core prices are steady, though, which gives the bank less reason to hurry.
boe.watch: Governor Andrew Bailey speaks Wednesday, November 18 at 9:00 AM CT, and UK retail sales follow Friday, November 20 at 1:00 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

USD.summary: The dollar sits third on the board. High US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh a little. A December Fed hike is seen as near certain, keeping the dollar near its highest since April 2025.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Cheaper oil helps the euro area, but budget worries in France and rates below most of the others hold it back. Rising US rates have pushed it to its lowest since April 2025, just under $1.10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board, level with the Aussie, because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight. UK inflation rose to 3.6% in October as forecast, which keeps a second Bank of England hike in December likely.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others and inflation is close to the Bank of Japan's goal. A likely December rate hike and warnings from Japan's finance minister only just keep the dollar below 160 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. The dollar has climbed to its highest against it in about 18 months.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, level on points with the pound, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Faster pay growth supports it, but falling gold and nervous markets have pushed it to its lowest since January.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Falling oil prices hurt Canada's exports, and recent Canadian data has mostly missed forecasts. The US dollar is close to its October high against it.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits fourth, in the middle of the board. Firm prices for New Zealand's dairy exports help, but doubts over a December rate hike have pushed it to its lowest since 2020.
